routes.label: Find the smallest possible prime in the pair

question:
The stronger Goldbach conjecture states that any even integer greater than \(7\) can be written as the sum of two different prime numbers. For such representations of the even number \(126,\) the largest possible difference between the two primes is

Note: The regular Goldbach conjecture states that any even integer greater than \(3\) is expressible as a sum of two primes. Neither this conjecture nor the stronger version has been settled.
solution:
With a fixed sum, the two primes are farthest apart when the smaller prime is as small as possible. Let \(p<q\) be primes with \(p+q=126\). Then
\[
q-p=126-2p,
\]
which decreases as \(p\) increases.

The primes smaller than \(13\) are \(2,3,5,7,11\). None works, because their required partners are composite:
\[
\begin{aligned}
126-2&=124=2\cdot62,\\
126-3&=123=3\cdot41,\\
126-5&=121=11^2,\\
126-7&=119=7\cdot17,\\
126-11&=115=5\cdot23.
\end{aligned}
\]
The next possibility is \(p=13\), giving \(q=113\). To verify that \(113\) is prime, it is enough to test prime divisors below \(11\), since \(113<11^2\). Indeed, a composite number must have a prime divisor at most its square root. The number \(113\) is divisible by none of \(2,3,5,7\); for the last test, \(113=7\cdot16+1\).

Thus \(13\) and \(113\) are an allowed pair, and every smaller candidate for \(p\) has been excluded. The maximum difference is
\[
113-13=\boxed{100},
\]
choice \(\text{B}\).

The evenness test supplies a useful contrast with the digit-sum test, preventing transfer of the last-digit rule to divisibility by three. The latter rule can be learned and checked independently, so preparation is useful without necessity.
